# Penguin

> Penguin is a funny pedometer and step counter app for iPhone (on the App Store: https://apps.apple.com/us/app/penguin-step-counter-pedometer/id6831137240), published by Lightbulb Moment Labs, Inc. Your daily steps from Apple Health power a smug, overconfident cartoon penguin. It's "the pedometer for people who hate pedometers." Now on the App Store.

Key facts:
- Platform: iPhone (iOS). Counts steps from Apple Health, so it works with just a phone or with an Apple Watch.
- Reads step count only. Step history stays on the device. No accounts, ads, analytics, or tracking.
- The penguin starts out pudgy (the couch bird) and gets fitter as you walk: couch bird, strong waddler, then athlete. It's framed as strength and confidence, never weight, and he never comments on the user's body.
- Daily step goal with rest days that never cost progress ("Aura").
- The Locker: unlockable outfits. Most are earned by walking; Penguin Plus adds Plus-only fits.
- Expeditions: an endless map of landmarks unlocked by steps.
- Waddles: small friend groups that share goal progress through iCloud and can send pokes.
- Pricing: free to download. The free version counts every step and includes the full glow-up, Aura, streaks, Waddles, widgets, and the first expedition. Penguin Plus ($39.99/year or $9.99/month, 7-day free trial on either plan) adds monthly drops of new fits, every expedition after the first (11 and counting, then endless victory laps), and Plus-only fits. Coming to Plus: Waddle challenges, a monthly Walk Wrapped recap, and customization (app icons, widget themes).
- Contact: gary@penguinathletics.com

## Learn: the health benefits of walking
Evidence-based, cited articles. Editorial policy: https://penguinathletics.com/learn/editorial-policy/

- [Walking and your heart](https://penguinathletics.com/learn/walking-heart-health/): Blood pressure, cholesterol, and the most underrated cardio on the planet.
- [Walking and longevity](https://penguinathletics.com/learn/walking-longevity/): How many steps buy you more years, and what the 10,000-step rule gets wrong.
- [Walking for weight loss](https://penguinathletics.com/learn/walking-weight-loss/): What walking really does for weight, blood sugar, and metabolism. No shame, just science.
- [Walking and your mind](https://penguinathletics.com/learn/walking-mental-health/): Stress, mood, sleep, and focus. A walk is the cheapest reset you own.
- [Walking basics](https://penguinathletics.com/learn/walking-basics/): How to start, stick with it, and maybe even like it. Built for people who hate exercise.

- [Walking for weight loss: the complete guide](https://penguinathletics.com/learn/walking-weight-loss/): Walking on its own usually leads to modest weight loss. In a review of pedometer-based walking programs with no diet changes, people lost about 1.3 kg (roughly 3 pounds) over a median of 16 weeks. Walking does more when paired with changes in eating, and it helps prevent weight gain and improves blood sugar and insulin sensitivity whatever the scale says.
- [Walking and your mind: the complete guide](https://penguinathletics.com/learn/walking-mental-health/): Walking is good for your mental health. A 2024 review of 75 trials found that walking reduced symptoms of depression and anxiety in adults, and people who move more tend to have a lower risk of depression. Walking works best alongside therapy or medication when you need them, not instead of them.
- [Walking and longevity: the complete guide](https://penguinathletics.com/learn/walking-longevity/): People who walk more tend to live longer. In a 2025 review of 57 studies, 7,000 steps a day was linked to a 47% lower risk of early death compared with 2,000 steps, and the benefits started to level off around 5,000 to 7,000 steps. Most of this evidence is observational, so it shows a strong link rather than proof, but walking is also linked to lower dementia risk and better function as you age.
- [Walking and your heart: the complete guide](https://penguinathletics.com/learn/walking-heart-health/): Walking is one of the best-studied ways to help your heart. In trials it lowered systolic blood pressure by about 4 mmHg, and in long-term studies people who walked the most had about 31% lower risk of cardiovascular disease than people who walked the least. Aim for about 150 minutes a week at a brisk pace, and start smaller if you need to.
- [Walking basics: the complete beginner's guide](https://penguinathletics.com/learn/walking-basics/): Adults need at least 150 minutes of moderate activity a week, and brisk walking counts. That's about 30 minutes a day, five days a week, at a pace where you can talk but not sing. If you're starting from zero, any amount helps, so begin small and build up gradually.
- [How to start walking when you hate exercise](https://penguinathletics.com/learn/how-to-start-walking-when-you-hate-exercise/): Start smaller than you think you need to, like a 5 to 10 minute walk tied to something you already do every day, and add a few minutes each week. Health guidelines say some activity is better than none and short walks count. New habits took about 66 days on average to feel automatic in one study, so aim for consistency, not intensity.
- [How many steps a day to live longer?](https://penguinathletics.com/learn/how-many-steps-a-day-to-live-longer/): In a pooled analysis of 15 studies, the risk of dying early kept falling as steps rose, then leveled off at about 6,000 to 8,000 steps a day for adults 60 and older and 8,000 to 10,000 for younger adults. You don't need 10,000 to benefit: a 2025 review linked 7,000 steps a day to a 47% lower risk of death than 2,000 steps.
- [How many steps a day do you need for heart health?](https://penguinathletics.com/learn/how-many-steps-a-day-do-you-need-for-heart-health/): You probably don't need 10,000. In large studies, people who took more steps had a lower risk of heart disease, with most of the benefit showing up by about 7,000 to 9,000 steps a day. In adults 60 and older, 6,000 to 9,000 steps a day was linked to a 40% to 50% lower risk of heart disease than about 2,000 steps.
- [Does walking lower blood pressure?](https://penguinathletics.com/learn/does-walking-lower-blood-pressure/): Yes. A large Cochrane review of 73 trials found that regular walking lowered systolic blood pressure (the top number) by about 4 mmHg on average. Most of the walking programs in those trials averaged around 150 minutes of moderate walking a week for a few months.
- [Does walking help anxiety?](https://penguinathletics.com/learn/does-walking-help-anxiety/): Yes, for many people it helps. A 2024 review of 26 trials in adults found that regular walking reduced anxiety symptoms compared with doing nothing, and a single bout of exercise can bring a small short-term drop too. Walking works best alongside therapy or medication when you need them, not instead of them.
- [Can you lose weight just by walking?](https://penguinathletics.com/learn/can-you-lose-weight-just-by-walking/): Yes, but usually only a little. In trials of walking alone, people lost about 1.4 kg (roughly 3 pounds) on average, and programs that combine walking with eating changes lead to more weight loss. Walking still improves blood pressure, blood sugar, and fitness even when the scale barely moves.
